z-m-01-01.title: Ways to share 9 marbles between two bags
z-m-01-01.topic: Splitting and combining numbers up to 10
z-m-01-01.goal: Show by making them yourself that there are many ways to split 9 into two numbers, and explain how to count them without missing any.
z-m-01-01.material: There are 9 marbles. You want to put all of them into two bags, a red bag and a blue bag, with none left over. Each bag gets at least 1 marble. The two bags are different colors, so you can tell them apart. Mina said, 'There is only one way to split 9 marbles between two bags.'
z-m-01-01.thinking.1: Making many ways that fit the conditions
z-m-01-01.thinking.2: Explaining how to count without missing or repeating any
z-m-01-01.prereq.0: Experience splitting and combining numbers up to 10 (Grade 1 level)
z-m-01-01.s.s1.prompt: What is a good way to find out whether Mina is right?
z-m-01-01.s.s1.hint.0: Say how many marbles are left for the blue bag when you put 1 marble in the red bag.
z-m-01-01.s.s1.hint.1: Change the number in the red bag to 2, then 3, and see what happens to the number left over.
z-m-01-01.s.s1.o.a: Count the 9 marbles again from the beginning
z-m-01-01.s.s1.r.a: It is already decided that there are 9 marbles. What you want to find out is how many ways there are to split them.
z-m-01-01.s.s1.o.b: Change the number of marbles in the red bag
z-m-01-01.s.s1.r.b: This idea is to change how you split and test for yourself whether there are other cases.
z-m-01-01.s.s1.o.c: Think there is only one way because there are two bags
z-m-01-01.s.s1.r.c: This idea treats the number of bags and the number of ways as the same thing. It did not look at what happens when the number in a bag changes.
z-m-01-01.s.s1.explain: The claim 'only one way' breaks as soon as even one other way appears. Test whether changing the number in the red bag also changes the number left for the blue bag.
z-m-01-01.s.s2.prompt: Split all 9 marbles so that the red bag has more marbles than the blue bag. Make 3 different ways. Each bag gets at least 1 marble.
z-m-01-01.s.s2.hint.0: Pick a number for the red bag, then count how many are left for the blue bag.
z-m-01-01.s.s2.hint.1: Choose the numbers while comparing whether the red bag's number is greater than the blue bag's number.
z-m-01-01.s.s2.var.r: Number of marbles in the red bag
z-m-01-01.s.s2.var.b: Number of marbles in the blue bag
z-m-01-01.s.s2.fail.c1: The number of marbles is a natural number, 1 or more. Put at least 1 marble in each bag.
z-m-01-01.s.s2.fail.c2: The marbles in the two bags must add up to 9.
z-m-01-01.s.s2.fail.c3: The red bag must have more marbles than the blue bag.
z-m-01-01.s.s2.explain: Putting 5, 6, 7, or 8 marbles in the red bag, all 4 ways are possible. Once the number in the red bag is set, the number in the blue bag is set too, so a different number in the red bag means a different way.
z-m-01-01.s.s3.prompt: If you tell the bags apart by color, how many ways are there in all to split 9 marbles between the two bags? Also write how you counted without missing or repeating any.
z-m-01-01.s.s3.hint.0: Decide the number in the red bag. Then how many are left for the blue bag?
z-m-01-01.s.s3.hint.1: Start with 1 in the red bag and increase it one at a time, writing it in a table or as number sentences, and check that you reached the end.
z-m-01-01.s.s3.selfAssess.0: Is the number of ways I counted the same as the number of ways I listed?
z-m-01-01.s.s3.selfAssess.1: Did you check that you did not count the same way twice or miss any?
z-m-01-01.s.s3.selfAssess.2: Did you notice that the answer changes depending on whether you tell the bags apart by color?
z-m-01-01.s.s3.model.0: I put 1, 2, 3, ... 8 marbles into the red bag in order and wrote what was left for the blue bag. It is 1+8, 2+7, ... 8+1, so there are 8 ways in all. If the colors are different, 5+4 and 4+5 are different ways.
z-m-01-01.s.s3.model.1: If we do not tell the colors apart, there are four ways: 1+8, 2+7, 3+6, 4+5. I wrote them while increasing one at a time, and I stopped when a pair with the same numbers as an earlier one came up, because that is the same way.
z-m-01-01.s.s3.modelNote.1: An interpretation that does not tell the colors apart is also valid if the reason is given.

z-m-01-02.title: When you count by 5s, is the last digit always 5?
z-m-01-02.goal: Learn that even if every example you saw is right, the claim 'always' is not guaranteed; find a number that breaks the last-digit claim and fix the claim properly.
z-m-01-02.material: Number cards are lined up in order from 0 to 100, counting by 5s. Chaewon looked at only the cards 5, 15, and 25 and said, 'When you count by 5s, the numbers you get always end in 5.' (0 is where counting by 5s starts, and this time we only think about the numbers from 5 to 100.)
z-m-01-02.thinking.0: Doubting a claim generalized from a few examples
z-m-01-02.thinking.2: Rewriting the claim to fit the conditions
z-m-01-02.prereq.0: Experience reading numbers up to 100 in order and counting by 5s
z-m-01-02.s.s1.prompt: Chaewon looked at only 5, 15, and 25 and said 'the last digit is always 5.' How should we treat what Chaewon said?
z-m-01-02.s.s1.hint.0: Count by 5s starting from 0 and write the first 8 or so numbers in order.
z-m-01-02.s.s1.hint.1: Among the numbers you wrote, mark the ones that are not the numbers Chaewon looked at (5, 15, 25).
z-m-01-02.s.s1.o.a: Since all three numbers were right, believe other numbers are always 5 too
z-m-01-02.s.s1.r.a: Even if all the numbers seen are right, there are still numbers not seen. This did not consider which numbers have not been seen yet.
z-m-01-02.s.s1.o.b: Say it is wrong because the three numbers being right was just luck
z-m-01-02.s.s1.r.b: Having examples that fit does not mean it is wrong. To say it is wrong, you need an example that breaks it.
z-m-01-02.s.s1.o.c: Count by 5s to the numbers not yet seen and check their last digits
z-m-01-02.s.s1.r.c: This idea is to test the numbers not seen and then decide.
z-m-01-02.s.s1.explain: The three numbers seen are only some of the numbers you get when counting by 5s. If you count the missing numbers yourself, you can tell whether the claim is always true.
z-m-01-02.s.s2.prompt: Counting by 5s from 0 gives 5, 10, 15, .... Among the numbers up to 100, write 2 different numbers whose last digit is not 5 to show that Chaewon's claim is wrong.
z-m-01-02.s.s2.hint.0: In 5, 10, 15, 20, ..., read just the last digits on their own.
z-m-01-02.s.s2.hint.1: Find where the last digit changes and write that number.
z-m-01-02.s.s2.var.n: A number you get when counting by 5s
z-m-01-02.s.s2.ok.c1: It is a number from 5 to 100.
z-m-01-02.s.s2.fail.c1: Write a number that is 5 or more and 100 or less.
z-m-01-02.s.s2.ok.c2: It is a number you get when counting by 5s.
z-m-01-02.s.s2.fail.c2: It is not a number you get when counting by 5s.
z-m-01-02.s.s2.ok.c3: The last digit is not 5. Chaewon's claim is broken.
z-m-01-02.s.s2.fail.c3: The last digit is 5. Look for a number whose last digit is not 5.
z-m-01-02.s.s2.explain: Numbers whose last digit is 0, like 10, 20, 30, also come up when counting by 5s. Even one example breaks the word 'always'.
z-m-01-02.s.s3.prompt: Fix what Chaewon said so it is correct about the last digits of the numbers you get when counting by 5s.
z-m-01-02.s.s3.hint.0: Write the last digits of 5, 10, 15, 20, 25, 30 on their own.
z-m-01-02.s.s3.hint.1: Look at what pattern the last digits repeat in and write it in one sentence.
z-m-01-02.s.s3.selfAssess.0: Did you check one by one that the fixed claim fits the numbers you wrote?
z-m-01-02.s.s3.selfAssess.1: Did you show with numbers why there are two possible last digits?
z-m-01-02.s.s3.selfAssess.2: Did you know when the word 'always' breaks when you used it?
z-m-01-02.s.s3.model.0: No. Numbers whose last digit is 0, like 10, 20, 30, come up too. When you count by 5s, the last digit is 5 or 0.
z-m-01-02.s.s3.model.1: If you count 5, 10, 15, 20, ..., the last digits are 5 and 0 taking turns, so it is not always 5.
z-m-01-02.s.s3.modelNote.1: An answer that also states the rule that they take turns.

z-m-01-03.title: Does changing the order give the same value?
z-m-01-03.topic: Switching the order in addition and subtraction
z-m-01-03.goal: Narrow down, bit by bit with new information, the range in which the claim 'changing the order gives the same value' is right, and find cases where the order cannot be switched.
z-m-01-03.material: Seoyun was talking about candies and said, 'When you calculate with two numbers, you get the same value even if you switch the order.' Let's look at the information one piece at a time and think about how far Seoyun's claim is right. Candies cannot be split or made from nothing, and you cannot eat more than you have.
z-m-01-03.thinking.0: Revising the range of a judgment when new information comes in
z-m-01-03.thinking.1: Finding the conditions under which a claim holds
z-m-01-03.thinking.2: Checking whether a calculation is possible after switching the order
z-m-01-03.prereq.0: Experience talking about putting together and taking away with numbers up to 10
z-m-01-03.s.s1.prompt: Look at the information one step at a time and see how your thinking about Seoyun's claim changes.
z-m-01-03.s.s1.hint.0: Find one thing that is different in the new information compared with the beginning.
z-m-01-03.s.s1.hint.1: Say in which cases Seoyun's claim is right and in which cases it is not.
z-m-01-03.s.s1.st.0.info: Put together a plate with 3 candies and a plate with 5 candies. 3 and 5 together make 8. If you switch the order and put together 5 and 3, it is also 8. Seoyun said, 'When you calculate with two numbers, you get the same value even if you switch the order.'
z-m-01-03.s.s1.st.0.ask: What do you think of Seoyun's claim based on what you have seen so far?
z-m-01-03.s.s1.st.0.after: We have only seen the putting-together case, so a careful idea like a or b is right. c made a firm statement about cases we have not seen.
z-m-01-03.s.s1.st.0.o.a: It seems so for putting together, but we need to look at other cases more
z-m-01-03.s.s1.st.0.r.a: This judgment separates the case we saw (putting together) from the cases we have not seen.
z-m-01-03.s.s1.st.0.o.b: There is only one pair of examples, so we cannot be sure even for putting together
z-m-01-03.s.s1.st.0.r.b: This judgment is careful about having few examples. It is the idea of checking with more examples.
z-m-01-03.s.s1.st.0.o.c: Believe it is always right for every calculation with two numbers
z-m-01-03.s.s1.st.0.r.c: This stretched the putting-together examples to every calculation. We have not yet looked at calculations that take away or find what is left.
z-m-01-03.s.s1.st.1.info: We looked at more putting-together examples. 4 and 6 make 10, and 6 and 4 also make 10. 0 and 7 make 7, and 7 and 0 also make 7. This time, think about eating 4 of 9 candies. 5 candies are left. If you switch the order, 'eating 9 from 4 candies' cannot be done, so this calculation would need a calculation we have not learned yet.
z-m-01-03.s.s1.st.1.ask: Based on what you have newly seen, what do you think of Seoyun's claim?
z-m-01-03.s.s1.st.1.after: The putting-together examples kept being right, and a case where the order cannot be switched appeared only in the eating case. A judgment that thinks separately about the range where the claim is right fits well.
z-m-01-03.s.s1.st.1.o.a: When putting together it is right, but when eating there are times you must not switch the order
z-m-01-03.s.s1.st.1.r.a: It separated the putting-together case and the eating case and narrowed the range where the claim is right.
z-m-01-03.s.s1.st.1.o.b: Whether putting together or eating, the value is always the same when you switch the order
z-m-01-03.s.s1.st.1.r.b: In the eating case, a situation appeared where switching the order makes the calculation impossible. Check again whether this fits that example.
z-m-01-03.s.s1.st.1.o.c: The eating example was wrong, so now we cannot trust the putting-together case either
z-m-01-03.s.s1.st.1.r.c: The eating example does not break the putting-together case. All three pairs of putting-together examples had the same value.
z-m-01-03.s.s1.st.2.info: Let's fix Seoyun's claim by adding a condition. Among the eating cases, if you eat 5 of 5 candies, 0 are left. In this case, even if you switch the order it is the same calculation, so it is 0. But there are cases where the order cannot be switched, like eating 4 of 9.
z-m-01-03.s.s1.st.2.ask: Choose the best way of fixing Seoyun's claim.
z-m-01-03.s.s1.st.2.after: Narrowing the range as in a, or separating the cases as in d, is a proper way to fix Seoyun's claim.
z-m-01-03.s.s1.st.2.o.a: When you put two numbers together, you get the same value even if you switch the order
z-m-01-03.s.s1.st.2.r.a: This is a statement narrowed to the case where the claim is right (putting together).
z-m-01-03.s.s1.st.2.o.b: For calculations with two numbers, whether putting together or eating, the value is always the same when you switch the order
z-m-01-03.s.s1.st.2.r.b: This statement stretches to every calculation even though there was an eating example where the order cannot be switched.
z-m-01-03.s.s1.st.2.o.c: If you just write the bigger number first, any calculation gives the same value when you switch the order
z-m-01-03.s.s1.st.2.r.c: If you write the bigger number first, there are cases where the switched calculation cannot be done at all. That is a different matter from whether switching the order gives the same value.
z-m-01-03.s.s1.st.2.o.d: When putting together it is the same, but when eating there are times you must not switch the order
z-m-01-03.s.s1.st.2.r.d: This statement separates the putting-together case and the eating case.
z-m-01-03.s.s1.reflect: The first information was only about putting together, so we could not know the range where the claim is right. As new information came in, did you come to separate the cases where it is right and the cases where it is not?
z-m-01-03.s.s2.prompt: For two numbers a and b from 0 to 20, find 2 different cases where both 'eating b from a' and 'eating a from b' can be done. (If the number you want to eat is more than the number you have, it cannot be done.)
z-m-01-03.s.s2.hint.0: Pick a and b, read each of the two calculations aloud in words, and check whether each can be done.
z-m-01-03.s.s2.hint.1: Compare which calculation cannot be done when a is greater than b and when a is less than b.
z-m-01-03.s.s2.fail.c1: Write both numbers as natural numbers from 0 to 20.
z-m-01-03.s.s2.ok.c2: You can eat b from a.
z-m-01-03.s.s2.fail.c2: To eat b from a, a must not be less than b.
z-m-01-03.s.s2.ok.c3: You can also eat a from b.
z-m-01-03.s.s2.fail.c3: You cannot eat a from b. b is less than a.
z-m-01-03.s.s2.explain: Only when the number you want to eat equals the number you have can both be done after switching the order, and then the number left is 0. You have to check first whether the calculation can be done after switching the order.

z-m-01-04.title: Does '=' always mean write the answer?
z-m-01-04.topic: The meaning of the equals sign (=)
z-m-01-04.goal: Find in a worked solution the misunderstanding that '=' is only a sign for writing the answer, and judge whether number sentences are true or false by the meaning that both sides are the same amount.
z-m-01-04.material: Jiho solved a problem to find the number that goes in □ in 3+4=□+2. Look at Jiho's solution line by line and think about what '=' shows. ('3+4' is read 'three plus four', and '□' is read 'box'.)
z-m-01-04.thinking.0: Finding the line that goes wrong in a solution
z-m-01-04.thinking.1: Correcting the meaning of a symbol
z-m-01-04.thinking.2: Calculating each side separately and comparing
z-m-01-04.prereq.0: Experience with simple calculations with numbers up to 10
z-m-01-04.s.s1.prompt: Jiho solved for the number in □ in 3+4=□+2 like this. Pick one line that is hard to believe.
z-m-01-04.s.s1.hint.0: Read each line aloud and see whether it follows naturally from the line before.
z-m-01-04.s.s1.hint.1: In the number sentence on line 3, calculate the left side 3+4 and the right side 7+2 separately and compare them.
z-m-01-04.s.s1.line.1: After = you write the result of the calculation, so write 7 in □.
z-m-01-04.s.s1.line.3: So □ is 7, and that is right.
z-m-01-04.s.s1.explain: Line 2 is the first problem. '=' does not always mean a result comes after it; it means the left side and the right side are the same amount. If you calculate the number sentence on line 3, the left side is 7 and the right side 7+2 is 9, so they are not the same. So the conclusion on line 4 is hard to believe too. What you see depends on the line you pick. Line 1 is calculated correctly.
z-m-01-04.s.s2.prompt: What does '=' mean? Choose the best answer.
z-m-01-04.s.s2.hint.0: Read 3+4=7 and 7=3+4 each aloud and see whether both make sense.
z-m-01-04.s.s2.hint.1: If there are 3+4 things on one side of a scale and □+2 things on the other side and it is level, say what relationship that is.
z-m-01-04.s.s2.o.a: It is a signal to write the answer on the right
z-m-01-04.s.s2.r.a: This idea sees '=' only as a place to write the answer. It is hard to explain number sentences written like 7=3+4.
z-m-01-04.s.s2.o.b: It is a signal to start calculating the left side
z-m-01-04.s.s2.r.b: This idea sees '=' as a command to calculate. It does not see that it is a sign for comparing whether both sides are the same.
z-m-01-04.s.s2.o.c: The left side and the right side are the same amount
z-m-01-04.s.s2.r.c: This idea sees it as a sign that both sides are the same amount.
z-m-01-04.s.s2.o.d: The number on the left is greater than the number on the right
z-m-01-04.s.s2.r.d: This idea cannot tell 'the same' from 'greater'. 'Greater' is shown with a different symbol.
z-m-01-04.s.s2.explain: '=' means both sides are the same amount. So in 3+4=□+2, you need to make □+2 the same amount as 3+4.
z-m-01-04.s.s3.prompt: Choose all the true number sentences below.
z-m-01-04.s.s3.hint.0: Calculate the left side and the right side of each number sentence separately and write them down.
z-m-01-04.s.s3.hint.1: If the two sides are the same, it is a true number sentence. If they are not the same, say which side is greater.
z-m-01-04.s.s3.r.a: Even when a calculation is on the right side of '=', the meaning of 'the same' does not change.
z-m-01-04.s.s3.r.b: The left is 7 and the right is 8, so they are not the same. This did not check that '=' means the same amount.
z-m-01-04.s.s3.r.c: Both sides are 7. Even when there are calculations on both sides, you can compare whether they are the same.
z-m-01-04.s.s3.r.d: This may be an idea that looked only at how many the left number increased by in the right-side calculation and decided they are the same. You have to calculate both sides separately and compare.
z-m-01-04.s.s3.explain: 7=3+4 is true because both sides are 7, and 6+1=5+2 is true because both sides are 7. 3+4=7+1 is 7 and 8, and 3+4=4+4 is 7 and 8, so they are not true.

z-m-01-05.title: Is it closer to 40 or to 50?
z-m-01-05.topic: Finding the nearest ten in numbers up to 100
z-m-01-05.goal: Compare closeness by the number of steps on a number line, learn about cases where you cannot say which is closer, and then make numbers that fit the conditions yourself.
z-m-01-05.material: Imagine 40, 41, 42, ..., 60 lined up one step apart on a number line. We compare how close two numbers are by how many steps apart they are on the number line. The fewer the steps, the closer. This time, think only about natural numbers.
z-m-01-05.thinking.0: Comparing closeness by the number of steps
z-m-01-05.thinking.1: Learning about cases where you cannot decide
z-m-01-05.thinking.2: Making many numbers that fit the conditions
z-m-01-05.prereq.0: Order and size comparison of numbers up to 100 (Grade 1 level)
z-m-01-05.s.s1.prompt: On a number line, 40, 41, 42, ..., 50 are lined up one step apart. Is 47 closer to 40 or to 50?
z-m-01-05.s.s1.hint.0: Count how many steps it is from 47 to the right to 50.
z-m-01-05.s.s1.hint.1: Also count how many steps it is from 47 to the left to 40, and compare.
z-m-01-05.s.s1.r.a: This judgment counted and compared the steps from 47 to each side.
z-m-01-05.s.s1.r.b: This may be the idea that the ten that comes first is closer. It did not count how many steps away 47 is from each.
z-m-01-05.s.s1.r.c: This idea did not compare the number of steps to the two places and just thought it is somewhere in the middle.
z-m-01-05.s.s1.explain: From 47 to 50 is 3 steps, and to 40 is 7 steps. The side with fewer steps is closer.
z-m-01-05.s.s2.hint.0: Count the steps from 45 to the left to 40 and to the right to 50, each separately.
z-m-01-05.s.s2.hint.1: Write the two numbers of steps side by side and compare which is greater.
z-m-01-05.s.s2.o.a: Closer to 50, because we agreed to round up when there is a 5
z-m-01-05.s.s2.r.a: An agreement is a different matter from closeness. It is not a reason based on counting and comparing steps.
z-m-01-05.s.s2.o.b: It is 5 steps from 40 and 5 steps from 50, so neither side is closer
z-m-01-05.s.s2.r.b: This judgment counted the steps to each of the two sides and compared them.
z-m-01-05.s.s2.r.c: This idea decided only by which number comes first or later. It did not count how many steps it is from 45 to each side.
z-m-01-05.s.s2.explain: From 45 to 40 is 5 steps, and to 50 is also 5 steps, so you cannot decide which is closer. In a case like this, we need an agreement about which way to send it.
z-m-01-05.s.s2.acc.0: If you follow the agreement 'round up when there is a 5', you can say 50. But that is an agreement we made, not because 45 is closer to 50. It is even better to say first that it is equally close to both.
z-m-01-05.s.s3.prompt: Write 3 different numbers that are greater than 40 and less than 60 and are closer to 50 than to 40 or 60.
z-m-01-05.s.s3.hint.0: Pick one candidate by comparing how many steps away from 50 it is with 40 and 60.
z-m-01-05.s.s3.hint.1: Find which of 40 and 60 your candidate has the same number of steps from, and leave that number out.
z-m-01-05.s.s3.ok.c1: It is a number greater than 40 and less than 60.
z-m-01-05.s.s3.fail.c1: Write a natural number greater than 40 and less than 60.
z-m-01-05.s.s3.ok.c2: It is closer to 50 than to 40.
z-m-01-05.s.s3.fail.c2: It is closer to 40 than to 50, or equally close to both.
z-m-01-05.s.s3.ok.c3: It is closer to 50 than to 60.
z-m-01-05.s.s3.fail.c3: It is closer to 60 than to 50, or equally close to both.
z-m-01-05.s.s3.explain: Every number from 46 to 54 fits the conditions. 45 and 55 are equally close to one of the tens, so they do not fit the condition 'closer'.

z-m-01-06.title: Can one number sentence fit many stories?
z-m-01-06.goal: Learn that one number sentence can show up in different stories (what is left, the difference), and make a story that fits a given number sentence yourself.
z-m-01-06.material: The number sentence 12-5 does not have to be shown by only one story. Look at what 12 and 5 mean in each story and what it asks to find, and pick the stories that fit the number sentence. Things are not split or made from nothing.
z-m-01-06.thinking.1: Finding many stories that show the same number sentence
z-m-01-06.thinking.2: Making a story that fits a number sentence
z-m-01-06.prereq.0: Experience counting numbers up to 20 and reading adding and taking-away stories
z-m-01-06.s.s1.prompt: Choose all the stories that fit the number sentence 12-5. (12-5 is read 'twelve minus five'.)
z-m-01-06.s.s1.hint.0: For each story, write what 12 and 5 each mean.
z-m-01-06.s.s1.hint.1: Compare whether what each story wants to find is 'a number greater than 12' or 'a number less than 12'.
z-m-01-06.s.s1.o.a: A child had 12 pencils and bought 5 more at the stationery store. How many pencils are there in all?
z-m-01-06.s.s1.r.a: This connected a story that gets bigger with the number sentence 12-5. Write the number sentence that fits the story again.
z-m-01-06.s.s1.o.b: 5 of 12 balloons popped. How many balloons are left?
z-m-01-06.s.s1.r.b: This connected a story where 5 are taken away from 12 with the number sentence.
z-m-01-06.s.s1.o.c: After eating 5 apples, 7 were left on the plate. How many apples were there at first?
z-m-01-06.s.s1.r.c: The number sentence is not 12-5 but '□-5=7'. A story that asks for the starting number is shown with a different number sentence.
z-m-01-06.s.s1.o.d: There are 12 red marbles and 5 blue marbles. How many more red marbles are there?
z-m-01-06.s.s1.r.d: You learned that a story that compares two numbers to find the difference can also be shown by 12-5.
z-m-01-06.s.s1.explain: The balloon story asks for the number left after 5 are gone from 12, and the marble story asks for the difference between 12 and 5. Both can be shown by 12-5. The pencil story is 12+5, and the apple story is □-5=7.
z-m-01-06.s.s2.prompt: Make up a story that fits the number sentence 9+6 yourself. Write it so it shows what 9 and 6 are in the story and what it asks. ('9+6' is read 'nine plus six'.)
z-m-01-06.s.s2.hint.0: First decide what 9 and 6 each count.
z-m-01-06.s.s2.hint.1: Think of one situation where two numbers are put together, and write the thing you want to ask in that situation as one question.
z-m-01-06.s.s2.selfAssess.0: Is it clear what 9 and 6 mean in my story?
z-m-01-06.s.s2.selfAssess.1: Is the answer to the question a number you find with 9+6?
z-m-01-06.s.s2.selfAssess.2: Is it a story that makes a friend think of 9+6 when they read it?
z-m-01-06.s.s2.model.0: There were 9 apples in a basket and Mom put in 6 more. How many apples are there in all?
z-m-01-06.s.s2.model.1: There were 9 children on the playground and 6 more came. How many children are on the playground now?
z-m-01-06.s.s2.modelNote.1: An answer that makes a putting-together situation into a story where things get bigger. A story that puts together two different groups is also good.

z-m-01-07.title: When you add, is it always more than at the start?
z-m-01-07.goal: Learn that to judge a claim you need the information 'how many are added', make a counterexample by adding 0, and fix the claim together with its condition.
z-m-01-07.material: There are 5 marbles in a marble box. Jian said, 'If you put more marbles in the marble box, there are always more marbles than at the start!' (Marbles are only put in, never taken out of the box. Putting in nothing can also be thought of as 'putting in 0 marbles'.)
z-m-01-07.thinking.0: Deciding what information is needed to judge
z-m-01-07.thinking.2: Fixing a claim by adding a condition
z-m-01-07.prereq.0: Experience counting and putting together numbers up to 10, and knowing that 0 means 'none at all'
z-m-01-07.s.s1.prompt: Jian said, 'If you put more marbles in the marble box, there are always more marbles than at the start.' What else do you need to know to tell whether this is right?
z-m-01-07.s.s1.hint.0: With 5 marbles in the box, think about the case of putting in 1 marble and the case of putting in 3 marbles.
z-m-01-07.s.s1.hint.1: Change the number of marbles you put in in different ways and find which numbers make the claim not right.
z-m-01-07.s.s1.o.a: What color the added marbles are
z-m-01-07.s.s1.r.a: Color has nothing to do with having more or fewer marbles. You need to find information that is related to the number of marbles.
z-m-01-07.s.s1.o.b: How big the marble box is
z-m-01-07.s.s1.r.b: Whether the box is big or small, the number of marbles in it can be counted separately. It is information that has nothing to do with whether there are more.
z-m-01-07.s.s1.r.c: This idea doubts that it may change depending on the number added.
z-m-01-07.s.s1.explain: The words 'put in more' do not say how many are put in. You need to know the number added to judge whether there are more than at the start.
z-m-01-07.s.s2.prompt: Choose the starting number of marbles and the number of marbles put in, and make 2 cases, with different starting numbers, where there are not more marbles than at the start. (The starting marbles are 1 or more and 20 or less.)
z-m-01-07.s.s2.hint.0: Change the number of marbles put in, and write down whether there are more than at the start.
z-m-01-07.s.s2.hint.1: Think about which number put in leaves the marbles in the box unchanged.
z-m-01-07.s.s2.ok.c1: The starting marbles are 1 or more and 20 or less.
z-m-01-07.s.s2.fail.c1: Write the starting marbles as a natural number from 1 to 20.
z-m-01-07.s.s2.ok.c2: The number of marbles put in is 0 or more.
z-m-01-07.s.s2.fail.c2: Write the number of marbles put in as a natural number that is 0 or more.
z-m-01-07.s.s2.ok.c3: There are not more marbles than at the start. Jian's claim is broken.
z-m-01-07.s.s2.fail.c3: There are more marbles than at the start. Choose the number put in again.
z-m-01-07.s.s2.explain: If 0 marbles are put in, the marbles stay just as they were. It is the same whatever the starting number is. So the claim 'if you put more in, it is always more' needs the condition 'if you put in even 1'.
z-m-01-07.s.s3.prompt: Rewrite Jian's claim correctly. Write it so it shows when the marbles are more than at the start and when they are not.
z-m-01-07.s.s3.hint.0: In the examples you made above, how many were put in? Say what happened to the marbles then.
z-m-01-07.s.s3.hint.1: Put the case of putting in 1 marble and the case of putting in 0 side by side and write one sentence.
z-m-01-07.s.s3.selfAssess.0: Does my fixed claim explain both the case of putting in 0 and the case of putting in 1 or more?
z-m-01-07.s.s3.selfAssess.1: Does it say the same thing whatever the starting number of marbles is?
z-m-01-07.s.s3.selfAssess.2: Did you write it with a 'condition' instead of 'always'?
z-m-01-07.s.s3.model.0: If you put in 1 or more, it is more than at the start. But if you put in 0, it stays the same.
z-m-01-07.s.s3.model.1: If you put in nothing, it does not grow and stays the same as at the start. If you put in even one, it gets more.
z-m-01-07.s.s3.modelNote.1: An answer that says the same meaning without the word '0'.

z-m-01-08.title: The number that goes in □: how can we trust it?
z-m-01-08.goal: Learn that values of □ found by different methods can be checked by one standard, putting the number you found in, then find a wrongly solved solution and tell a friend how to check.
z-m-01-08.material: In the number sentence □+6=14, □ is 'the number that makes 14 when you add 6'. Dohyeon found it by trying numbers in □ one at a time, and Sea found it by counting back 6 steps from 14. Gaon solved it a different way. ('□+6=14' is read 'box plus six is fourteen'.)
z-m-01-08.thinking.0: Checking different methods by the same standard
z-m-01-08.thinking.1: Finding the line that goes wrong in a solution
z-m-01-08.thinking.2: Explaining a way to check to a friend
z-m-01-08.prereq.0: Experience finding sums of numbers up to 20 and finding the number that makes a certain number when added
z-m-01-08.s.s1.prompt: In □+6=14, Dohyeon tried 7, 9, and 8 in □ in turn and found 8. Sea counted back 6 steps from 14 and found 8. What is right about the two methods?
z-m-01-08.s.s1.hint.0: Check whether the numbers the two found are the same.
z-m-01-08.s.s1.hint.1: Put the number you found, 8, into □, calculate 8+6, and see whether it makes 14.
z-m-01-08.s.s1.o.a: Only Dohyeon's method of trying numbers directly can be trusted
z-m-01-08.s.s1.r.a: This idea trusts only the method of trying numbers directly. Sea's method gave the same number too, and you can check it by putting it in.
z-m-01-08.s.s1.o.b: Only Sea's method of counting back is right
z-m-01-08.s.s1.r.b: This idea accepts only the counting-back method. Dohyeon's method was also checked by putting it in □.
z-m-01-08.s.s1.o.c: For both, you can check by putting 8 in □
z-m-01-08.s.s1.r.c: This judgment sees that both methods can be checked by the same standard (whether putting it in □ makes 14).
z-m-01-08.s.s1.explain: Trying numbers and counting back are different paths, but they found the same number, 8. Whichever method you use, you can trust the number if you put it in □ and check that 8+6=14.
z-m-01-08.s.s2.prompt: Gaon found □ in □+6=14 like this. Pick one line that is hard to believe.
z-m-01-08.s.s2.hint.0: First estimate whether □ is likely to be a number greater than 14 or less than 14.
z-m-01-08.s.s2.hint.1: Think about whether □ is less than or greater than 14, and compare whether line 2 fits that estimate.
z-m-01-08.s.s2.line.0: If you add 6 to □ you get 14, he said.
z-m-01-08.s.s2.line.1: So you put 14 and 6 together to find □.
z-m-01-08.s.s2.explain: Line 2 is the first problem. If adding 6 to □ made 14, then adding 6 more to 14 gives a number greater than □. So □=20 on line 4 is hard to believe too. What you see depends on the line you pick. Line 1 is correct because it turned the number sentence into words.
z-m-01-08.s.s3.prompt: Write, as words telling Gaon, a way Gaon can check by himself whether □=20 is right.
z-m-01-08.s.s3.hint.0: Put the 20 Gaon found in the place of □ and calculate the left side.
z-m-01-08.s.s3.hint.1: Put the result of your calculation next to the 14 on the right, compare whether they are the same, and tell Gaon.
z-m-01-08.s.s3.selfAssess.0: Did you write it in order so Gaon can follow it?
z-m-01-08.s.s3.selfAssess.1: Did you write what calculation you do when you put in 20?
z-m-01-08.s.s3.selfAssess.2: Did you say whether the result is the same as or different from 14?
z-m-01-08.s.s3.model.0: Put 20 in the place of □ and calculate 20+6. It is 26, so it is not 14. So 20 is wrong.
z-m-01-08.s.s3.model.1: Let's put in 20. 20+6=26, which is different from 14, so it is wrong. If you put in another number, 8, then 8+6=14, so it is right.
z-m-01-08.s.s3.modelNote.1: An answer that checks the wrong number and then also tries the right number.
